entries.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Thin on his own words, strong on his death. The Library holds one letter by him, to the church at Philippi. It also holds the Smyrna church's own account of his death. Irenaeus and Eusebius add what they knew of him.

His letter is accepted as his own, though some scholars argue that its thirteenth chapter was added later. The year of his death is argued. Most scholars now say about 155. Jerome and the Chronicle of Eusebius point to 167.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity, which holds his letter. Two of its links give what Irenaeus says of him. They deal with Marcion and Valentinus.
entries.why: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna in Asia. His letter to the church at Philippi survives. Irenaeus saw him in his early youth and called him a pupil of the apostles. Polycarp died at Smyrna for refusing to curse Christ.
entries.teaser: Smyrna, c. 110 to 155 CE: an old bishop who told the proconsul he had served Christ eighty-six years, and would not curse him.
entries.longDescription:
Irenaeus saw Polycarp in his early youth. He says apostles in Asia made Polycarp bishop there. He says Polycarp lived a very long time and taught what he had learned from the apostles. Irenaeus could still describe the place where Polycarp sat and taught.

Polycarp wrote to the church at Philippi, in his own name and that of the presbyters with him. He had Ignatius's letters and sent them on to Philippi. In Rome, Irenaeus says, Polycarp turned many away from Marcion and Valentinus. He also met Marcion once. Marcion asked, “Dost thou know me?” Polycarp answered, “I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.” He and Anicetus, bishop of Rome, disagreed about the keeping of Easter. Neither could persuade the other, yet they kept communion.

At Smyrna the proconsul told him to swear and to reproach Christ. Polycarp answered, “Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?” The church of Smyrna wrote that the fire could not consume his body, so an executioner pierced him with a dagger.
voices: Polycarp of Smyrna — bishop, whose letter to the church at Philippi the Library holds
Irenaeus of Lyon — who saw Polycarp in his youth and wrote down what he remembered of him
entries.legacy:
Two later traditions name him. The church historians Socrates and Sozomen tell of his Easter dispute with the bishop of Rome. Sozomen says that bishop was Victor. The Library's note says it was Anicetus.

The Anabaptists' Martyrs' Mirror tells his death at length. It has him tell the governor, “I have now served my Lord Christ Jesus eighty-six years.”

entries.name: Methodius of Olympus
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, his fragments and a treatise On Free Will. Its introduction calls the Banquet the only complete work of his that survives. It says critics doubt that On Free Will is his.

Some sayings later writers give him may not be his. The editors also flag one work that Nikon cites under his name.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within The Anatolian Church in the Third Century, whose Library shelf holds his works. Two links of that entry name him: his books against Origen, and Jerome's list of his works.
entries.why: Methodius was a bishop in Lycia. He wrote the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, a dialogue that praises virginity. Its frame comes from Plato's Symposium. He also wrote against Origen. He died a martyr about 312.
entries.teaser: Olympus in Lycia, c. 290 to 312 CE: a bishop who had ten women speak on chastity, and who wrote against Origen.
entries.longDescription:
The sources do not agree on his sees. Jerome says Methodius was bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre. The Library's introduction says he held Olympus and Patara together. It puts his martyrdom about the year 312, at the end of the last great persecution.

His best-known book is the Banquet of the Ten Virgins. Ten women meet for a feast. Arete, whose name means Virtue, asks each one to speak in praise of virginity. Marcella, the eldest, speaks first. The Library's introduction calls it a dialogue of considerable power and grace.

Methodius also wrote against Origen. Jerome lists On the Resurrection and On Free Will as aimed at him. Photius, a later reader, says the first holds that the body is not the soul's fetter. Yet the Library's introduction says Origen's way of reading Scripture shaped him too.
voices: Methodius of Olympus — bishop and author of the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, whose works the Library holds
Jerome — who lists his books in his catalog of Christian writers
entries.legacy:
Later churches quote him as an early witness. In the Russian church, Nikon's replies to Streshnev and Ligarides quote a gloss on Revelation that gives Methodius's words. They say the woman clothed with the sun is the Church.

In the Catholic Church of the old regime, Liguori's Glories of Mary quotes words he gives to “St. Methodius the martyr” in praise of Mary.

Jerome lists the Banquet by name in his catalog of Christian writers. Whether he drew on it is not shown.

entries.name: Lactantius
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds four works of his own on the shelf of the Latin Apologists: the Divine Institutes, On the Workmanship of God, A Treatise on the Anger of God, and fragments. They come in Latin and in English.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. Jerome admired his style more than his teaching. He wished Lactantius had been as ready to teach Christian doctrine as to pull down other men's.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within The Latin Apologists, the entry whose line of writers ends with him. Two of its links name him: one where he says Tertullian had already argued the same cause, and one where Jerome has him teach Constantine's son.
entries.why: Lactantius taught rhetoric. Jerome says he was called to Nicomedia in the reign of Diocletian. Pupils were few there, so he took up writing. He wrote in Latin to defend the faith. His Divine Institutes open with an address to Constantine.
entries.teaser: Nicomedia and Gaul, c. 303 to 325 CE: a teacher of Latin rhetoric who turned to writing when his pupils were few, and addressed his defence of the faith to Constantine.
entries.longDescription:
Jerome calls him Firmianus, known also as Lactantius, and a pupil of Arnobius. In the reign of Diocletian he was summoned to Nicomedia to teach rhetoric. It was a Greek city, so he had few pupils. He turned to writing.

Jerome lists his books. They include a Banquet written as a young man in Africa, a verse Itinerary of a journey from Africa to Nicomedia, and a book On the Anger of God. Another is the Divine Institutes, in seven books. It begins, “We undertake, therefore, to discuss religion and divine things.” It is addressed to Constantine, the first of the Roman princes, Lactantius says, to give up errors and honour the one true God. In it he says Tertullian had already argued the same cause in full.

In extreme old age, Jerome says, Lactantius taught Crispus, a son of Constantine, in Gaul. Constantine later put Crispus to death. An editor's note in the Library puts the death of Lactantius at 325.
voices: Lactantius — teacher of rhetoric and Christian writer, whose Divine Institutes, treatises and fragments the Library holds
Jerome — who lists his books and says he taught the son of Constantine
entries.legacy:
Two later traditions name him. Jerome, in his letters, says Lactantius has “a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully”, meaning Cicero. He adds a wish that Lactantius had been as ready to teach Christian doctrines as to pull down those of others. His catalog of Christian writers lists his books.

Calvin cites him too. In the Institutes he ends one argument “with Lactantius”, that no religion is genuine if it does not agree with truth. On images, he tells readers to read Lactantius and Eusebius. A letter in his collected letters calls Lactantius “an ancient doctor of the Church.”

Polycarp's Socrates passage also says he died under Gordian, which the Library's note corrects.

POLYCARP, Easter dispute: the long dispute figures in two Library sources (Eusebius HE V.24 quoting Irenaeus; Socrates V.22). Eusebius's editor notes the meaning of Anicetus's 'conceding the eucharist' is disputed; the entry does not state it.

METHODIUS, sees and death: the Library gives Olympus and Patara (Library introduction, citing Jerome) while Jerome says Olympus and afterwards Tyre; it places his death at Chalcis, Greece or Syria, about 312, and says the claim of a death under Decius and Valerian is incorrect. The entry gives the first two and the date. The Library's 'about 312' and Jerome's editor's note 'died 311 or 312' agree with the census 'around 311'.

METHODIUS, later traditions: the Russian count rests on a quoted gloss on Revelation inside Nikon's replies, not Nikon's own sentences (the count's doubts). The legacy says exactly that. Palmer's note says one Methodius work Nikon cites is quoted erroneously; Liguori's sayings may include words now given to pseudo-Methodius. sourcing says 'some sayings later writers give him may not be his' and does not say which. The Nikon text is an OCR file; the quoted passage is taken verbatim from it.

LACTANTIUS, place: region 'Nicomedia, Gaul' (Jerome's words). modernCountries is empty because no census entry carries Nicomedia or Gaul and I do not type IDs from memory. regions is Asia Minor and Mediterranean, not the home's three.

LACTANTIUS, concerns: both links in links_naming_person had concerns null and are set to lactantius in the concerns list. In tertullian-s-voice--latin-apologists the person the sources quote is Lactantius (it is his sentence about Tertullian). The link's from end is tertullian-s-voice, but that does not change whose words the sources are.

LEGACY, Calvin letter: the Calvin letters line cited (calvin_letters-vol1_bonnet1858.txt, line 16669) is a 1543 letter in Calvin's collected letters; the OCR heading names the curate of Cernex as the recipient. The legacy says only 'a letter in his collected letters'.
